rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical peak pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to measure how the unresolved first pair responds to slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, allowing better resolution without a substantial time penalty.

The critical first pair improved only slightly with a shallower gradient, so test temperature-driven selectivity while holding the gradient fixed. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving room for further resolution optimization.
Injection 3 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keeping temperature at 60 C preserves the selectivity that resolved the first pair.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover baseline resolution of the first pair while retaining a 10-minute gradient. This slope lies between injections 3 and 4 and should achieve full resolution with earlier final elution than injection 3.

Raise the gradient window while preserving injection 5’s slope to test whether initial solvent strength can shorten elution without losing full resolution. Injection 5 remains the fully resolved fallback if the first pair becomes compressed.

Test the opposite temperature extreme to see whether it separates the critical pair in the other elution order. If lower temperature provides more selectivity, a steeper gradient may yield a faster fully resolved method.

Test whether a modest temperature increase separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while retaining adequate separation of the first pair. Shortening the gradient simultaneously explores a faster alternative to the fully resolved 60 C method.

Return to the successful high-temperature selectivity and trim the gradient window, placing its endpoint above the last peak’s estimated elution composition. This slope is only slightly steeper than injection 5, targeting full resolution with a shorter gradient and slightly earlier final elution.

Test a slightly steeper, shorter gradient near the first pair’s resolution limit. The final peak may elute shortly into the hold, so this run will establish whether the trimmed endpoint preserves both full resolution and rapid elution.

Explore an alternative selectivity window: 35 C should spread the late cluster relative to 30 C, while the higher starting organic fraction shortens retention and may improve the early pair’s selectivity. Keep injection 10 as the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the unresolved first pair at 35 C, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention. This tests whether the alternative temperature window can deliver full resolution with faster elution.

At 30 C the first pair has better selectivity than at 35 C; a shallower gradient should also help separate the late cluster. The raised starting fraction offsets some of the retention increase while testing another route to full resolution.

Return to 60 C and reduce the slope relative to injection 6 to recover first-pair resolution. This tests whether a modestly raised starting fraction can produce a fully resolved method near the current fastest result.

Reduce the slope from 0.075 to 0.070 organic fraction per minute to bring the first pair above R = 1.5. This should establish a fully resolved alternative with a higher starting organic fraction and final elution near seven minutes.

Test the next steeper slope near the first pair’s resolution boundary, between the successful injection 10 and underresolved injection 4. This may shorten final elution while retaining the maximum CRF; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a shallower gradient and lower starting fraction at 35 C to improve the early pair while preserving separation of the late cluster. This explores a lower-temperature route to maximum CRF, with the proven 60 C methods retained as fallbacks.

Keep nearly the same slope as injection 17 while raising the endpoint so the final peak elutes during the gradient rather than the hold. The first pair should remain fully resolved, and removing the hold-related delay should bring the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the temperature sensitivity of injection 10, the fastest fully resolved method so far. Its first-pair resolution margin is small, so this run will establish whether a 5 C reduction preserves the maximum CRF or requires a shallower gradient.

Preserve injection 3’s successful slope and temperature while trimming the endpoint and programmed gradient duration. The last peak should still elute during the gradient, retaining maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 10.

Fine-tune the slope just above injection 15’s value, targeting first-pair resolution at the full-credit threshold with slightly earlier final elution. Although the programmed gradient is longer, all peaks should elute well before its endpoint.

Test a shallower gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already established; this run seeks a less marginal fully resolved alternative to the fastest method, injection 10.

Steepen injection 22 slightly to shorten elution while retaining a useful resolution margin above 1.5. This targets a faster, comfortably resolved alternative, while injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Use a slope between injections 20 and 23 to shorten elution relative to injection 23 while retaining more resolution margin than injection 10. The endpoint should remain above the last peak’s elution composition, avoiding hold-related delay.

Use a slope between injections 20 and 24 to retain a clear resolution margin while keeping final elution below eight minutes. The campaign has already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000; injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
